title: Marco Polo on the Silk Road
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA + OBJECTS_IN_AREA on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR reaching area (100,52)-(116,68); count 1, player 1, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "VC Victory"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "Defeat Marco Dead"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 1, player 1, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "Defeat Caravan Lost"]
issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero - a Norman duke of the 11th century, an entirely unrelated culture and era; a renamed generic unit (or even a Trade Cart escort figure) was available and would have been correct.
Niccolo Polo is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian warlord - again wrong culture and wrong century for a 13th-century Venetian merchant.

GENGHIS_KHAN is placed (under GAIA) at the destination, apparently standing in for Kublai Khan. Genghis died in 1227, decades before the journey and before Shangdu was built; the text explicitly names Kublai, so the placed hero contradicts the narration.

Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the castle, keep and archery range architecture is unspecified and could render as any culture from Britons to Aztecs - avoidable, since Mongols/Persians/Chinese/Turks were all selectable.

The caravan's 'pack animals' are SHEEP, when the engine ships Trade Carts (and camels) that would read far better as a Silk Road merchant caravan; the escort of KNIGHTS and CROSSBOWMEN is a European field force rather than hired caravan guards.
GAIA-owned CASTLE and KEEPs with PALISADE_WALL fragments are an odd, unexplained fortification set for either a Persian oasis or Shangdu's summer palace.
strengths: The route is staged in the correct order with correct place-names: Persian oasis, the Pamir ('Roof of the World'), the Taklamakan wastes, then Shangdu.
Narration is factually sound on dates and details - 1271 departure, Marco aged seventeen, three years of travel, seventeen years in Kublai's service.
Steppe bandits built from CAVALRY_ARCHER, LIGHT_CAVALRY and SCOUT_CAVALRY with yurt encampments is a culturally apt and engine-appropriate raider force.
Victory conditions encode the actual historical task - deliver the traveller alive to Shangdu with the caravan's animals intact - rather than defaulting to destroying the enemy.
Defeat on losing the last pack animal reflects the real stake of a trade caravan, whose goods and gifts were the reason for the journey.
justification: The scenario's structure and text are genuinely faithful: an escort journey through Persia, the Pamir and the Taklamakan to Shangdu, with dates, ages and durations that match the sources, and a victory condition gated on bringing the protagonist to the Khan's palace with at least one pack animal surviving - exactly the historical objective. The casting, however, is badly wrong in avoidable ways: Marco is William the Conqueror and Niccolo is El Cid, two 11th-century figures from unrelated cultures, and Genghis Khan is placed at the destination in place of the Kublai Khan the text names. Both players are left on RANDOM civilization, so the architecture at the oasis and at Shangdu is arbitrary, and the caravan's goods are sheep rather than the Trade Carts the engine offers.

issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero — an 11th-century Norman duke, wrong culture and two centuries out of period; a renamed generic unit (villager, trade cart driver, or even a Genoese/Italian militia unit) was available and would have been correct.
Niccolo Polo is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian warlord on horseback, again wrong culture and era for a Venetian merchant.

GENGHIS_KHAN is placed (as GAIA, near the Shangdu castle/keeps) while all narration names Kublai Khan; Genghis died in 1227, 44 years before the journey begins. Same dynasty and culture, but the wrong Khan, and the engine offers no alternative so the substitution is a lesser but still avoidable framing error.

Escort composition of KNIGHTS and CROSSBOWMEN reads as a Western European war band rather than the hired local guides and guards the Polos actually travelled with.

The 'Defeat Caravan Lost' condition tests OBJECTS_IN_AREA count 1 for player 1 over the entire map rather than the sheep specifically, so it is only loosely tied to the pack animals it claims to track.
strengths: Route staging is faithful and in correct order: Persian oasis, the Pamir 'Roof of the World', then approach to Shangdu, matching the itinerary of the Travels.
Bandit ambush triggers fired by caravan movement reflect the real hazard of raiders (Marco's Karaunas) preying on caravans in the deserts of Persia and Central Asia.
Victory encodes the actual historical goal: bring Marco alive to Shangdu with at least one pack animal surviving; defeat is Marco's death or loss of the caravan — not a generic 'destroy the enemy'.
Environmental dressing is period- and place-appropriate: yurts for the steppe player, tents and a pavilion for the caravan camp, palm forest, cliffs, rock formations for desert and mountain passes.
Narration is chronologically accurate: 1271 departure, Marco aged seventeen, three thousand miles, three years of travel, seventeen years in the Khan's service.
justification: The scenario's route, hazards and win/lose logic are genuinely well matched to the Polos' journey — dialogue-gated stages at the Persian oasis, the Pamir, and Shangdu, bandit patrols triggered by caravan movement, and a victory that turns on delivering Marco alive with at least one pack animal, exactly the historical stake. The casting, however, is badly wrong in avoidable ways: Marco is William the Conqueror and Niccolo is El Cid, both 11th-century Western European warlords, when a renamed generic unit was available, and the figure waiting at Shangdu is Genghis Khan while every line of text names Kublai. Both players are left on RANDOM civilization, so the architecture and rosters are unassigned despite an otherwise plausible desert-and-yurt setting, and the caravan's goods are sheep rather than the trade carts the engine ships. The written content a player reads is accurate and informative; the objects they command are not.

Niccolo Polo is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian warlord — again wrong culture and wrong century, and avoidable.

The Polo escort is composed of KNIGHTs and CROSSBOWMEN belonging to the same player as the merchants; a 17-year-old's family trade party crossing Asia under Mongol safe-conduct was not a heavy-cavalry column.

Genghis Khan is placed under GAIA rather than as an active player, so the Khan's court is scenery with no agency in the encounter.
strengths: Bandit forces are CAVALRY_ARCHER, LIGHT_CAVALRY and SCOUT_CAVALRY — an appropriate mounted-steppe-raider composition for Karaunas-style caravan predation Marco himself describes.

Terrain and props (TREE_PALM_FOREST, ROCK_FORMATION, CLIFF sets, YURT_A-D for the raider camp, TENT/PAVILION for the caravan) read plausibly as desert and mountain Central Asia.

Victory is gated on the specific person reaching the specific place (Marco's unit inside the Shangdu area) with at least one pack animal surviving, and defeat on Marco's death or total loss of the caravan — exactly the stakes the journey posed.
Narration is factually sound on dates and outcome: departure 1271, roughly three years on the road, and Marco's subsequent seventeen years in the Khan's service.
justification: The trigger design is the strongest part of this scenario: victory turns on escorting one named individual to Shangdu with pack animals intact, and defeat on his death or the caravan's loss, which is precisely the historical stake and avoids the generic 'kill the enemy' default. The casting, however, is badly wrong in avoidable ways — William the Conqueror plays Marco Polo, El Cid plays Niccolo, and Genghis Khan (dead 44 years before the journey) sits at a court the text explicitly attributes to Kublai, when renamed generic units were available. Both players are left on RANDOM civilization, so the architecture of a Silk Road scenario is a coin flip despite the well-chosen yurt and palm-desert scenery. The staged route (Persia, Pamir, Taklamakan, Shangdu) and the steppe-raider composition are accurate, and the narration's dates hold up.

title: The Battle of Hastings
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 2) [path "[VC] Victory - Harold Slain"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "[Defeat] William Slain"]
  - TIMER + OBJECTS_IN_AREA on 1800s elapsed; count 1, player 2, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "[Defeat] Nightfall"]
issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so architecture, unit skins and bonuses could resolve to Aztec, Japanese or Mongol - avoidable, since Franks/Britons were available for Normans and Saxons respectively
2,560 oak trees dominate a 120x120 map; Senlac Hill was an open ridge fronted by a shallow valley, and a dense forest is the wrong tactical stage for cavalry charges and feigned retreats
Both armies are given Town Centers, Monasteries and Barracks; Hastings was a one-day field engagement with no settlement, fortification or production base on either side

Norman force (10 knights, 10 archers, 10 spearmen) is barely half the Saxon strength (20 champions, 20 spearmen, 10 skirmishers), whereas the sources put the two hosts at roughly comparable size, with the Normans holding the advantage in horse and bow
The 'Norman Reinforcements' trigger ('Fresh Norman riders arrive from the coast') is an invention - William committed his whole army at Hastings and received no reinforcement during the battle
Saxon skirmishers overstate Anglo-Saxon missile capability; Harold's army is noted for having almost no archers at Hastings
Harold is represented by the generic KING unit, an immobile non-combatant, rather than a renamed fighting unit - the historical Harold fought in the shield wall
strengths: William the Conqueror is the correct engine hero for the correct person, side and year - no anachronistic hero substitution
Saxon line built from CHAMPION (axe-armed housecarls) and SPEARMAN is an appropriate abstraction of the shield wall within the engine's catalogue
The feigned-retreat mechanic is implemented as triggers, not just narration: OBJECTS_IN_AREA fires a Saxon PATROL downhill, then an 'Ambush Springs' trigger destroys the isolated pursuers
Victory is gated on killing Harold specifically, and defeat on either William's death or the sun setting with the Saxons intact - exactly the two conditions the day actually turned on
Date, place and personalities in the narration are correct (14 October 1066, Senlac Hill, Harold Godwinson, housecarls)
justification: The scenario encodes the historical problem almost perfectly: kill Harold before nightfall, lose if William dies or the shield wall survives the day, with the feigned retreat and downhill pursuit ambush actually implemented in triggers rather than merely described. Combatants are strong - the correct William hero, champions and spearmen standing in for the housecarl shield wall - though the Norman force is oddly outnumbered and Harold is a static KING unit. The setting is the weak point: both civilizations are left RANDOM, so the Normans may appear as Aztecs, and the battlefield is buried under 2,560 oak trees with Town Centers and Monasteries on a map that should be an open ridge. The invented seaborne cavalry reinforcement is the only factual assertion the sources do not support.

  - TIMER + OBJECTS_IN_AREA on 1800s elapsed; count 1, player 2, area (0,0)-(119,119) [path "[Defeat] Nightfall"]
issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so Norman and Anglo-Saxon architecture, unit bonuses and tech are left to chance; Franks/Britons (or Celts for the axe-wielding housecarls) were available and would have fixed the visual and tactical identity.
2,560 oak trees on a 120x120 map turns Senlac into dense woodland; the battle was fought on an open chalk ridge with the Andredsweald only at the Saxon rear.
No terrain elevation or hill is evident in the placed content, yet 'Senlac Hill' and the uphill charge are the entire tactical premise of the brief and the dialogue.

Harold Godwinson is represented by an unmodified generic KING unit; the sources' Harold fought on foot in the shield wall with his housecarls, and the King unit is a fleeing non-combatant in engine terms.

Norman force (10 knights, 10 archers, 10 spearmen) is badly outnumbered by the Saxon 20 champions + 20 spearmen + 10 skirmishers, inverting the roughly parity of numbers at Hastings and giving the attacker no weight of cavalry.
Anglo-Saxon SKIRMISHER x10: Harold's army was famously almost devoid of missile troops at Hastings, having outrun its archers from Stamford Bridge.
'Norman Reinforcements ... Fresh Norman riders arrive from the coast' is invented; no reinforcement reached William during the battle - his entire force was already engaged.
Both defeat triggers (William Slain, Nightfall) fire DECLARE_VICTORY, so the losing outcomes are mechanically declared as wins.
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the engine's correct hero for the Norman commander, placed with the Norman player.
Victory is gated on destroying Harold (the KING of player 2), which is exactly the decision point of the historical battle.
Defeat on William's death reflects the real crisis in which the rumour of William's fall nearly broke the Norman host, and he had to bare his head to rally them.
The nightfall timer defeat correctly encodes the historical deadline: the Normans had to break the wall before dark or the invasion failed.
The feigned-retreat sequence (Feigned Retreat Hint -> Saxon Pursuit patrol -> Ambush Springs) reproduces the reported breaking of ranks and the destruction of pursuing Saxons on the slope.
Saxon CHAMPION units are a reasonable engine stand-in for axe-armed housecarls, and the Norman combined archer/knight/spearman mix matches William's three-arm army.
Date, place and named protagonists in the narration (14 October 1066, near Hastings, William and Harold Godwinson) are accurate.
justification: The scenario gets the shape of Hastings right: William as a named hero, Harold as the assassination target, a nightfall deadline, and a scripted feigned retreat that lures Saxon spearmen off the ridge into an ambush - all of which make the encoded win condition the historical one. The setting is the weak link: both civilizations are left RANDOM so neither Norman nor Saxon architecture is guaranteed, 2,560 oak trees bury an open chalk ridge in forest, and no elevation is placed for the 'Senlac Hill' the entire premise depends on. Force composition also drifts - the attacking Normans are outnumbered 30 to 51, and the Saxons are given ten skirmishers despite their notorious lack of missile troops - while the 'fresh Norman riders from the coast' reinforcement trigger asserts something no source supports.

title: The Battle of Tours
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on SALADIN (player 2) [path "[VC] Abd al-Rahman Slain"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 3, player 3, area (40,92)-(80,115) [path "[VC] Umayyad Withdrawal"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (player 1) [path "[Loss] Charles Martel Killed"]
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 10, player 2, area (40,15)-(80,35) [path "[Loss] Shield Wall Overrun"]
issues_found: Charles Martel is represented by the WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR hero — a Norman duke of 1066, three centuries later and a different polity; a renamed generic Frankish champion/paladin would have been the correct substitution.

Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi is represented by SALADIN, a 12th-century Kurdish Ayyubid sultan — wrong dynasty, wrong culture, wrong century by over 450 years, and the victory trigger is literally keyed on DESTROY_OBJECT of SALADIN.
Duke Odo of Aquitaine is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian — wrong realm and era; a renamed generic knight would have been better.

Both active players are set to civilization RANDOM, so architecture and unit bonuses are unassigned; Franks (and a Saracen/Berber-flavoured civ for the Umayyads) were available and would have fixed the building set.

Player 3 (Odo) is given SCOUT_CAVALRY and KNIGHT with no infantry at all; the Aquitanian contingent that raided the camp was a mixed force, and the tiny 20-unit armies understate a battle of tens of thousands even allowing for scale abstraction.
Umayyad roster leans on CAMEL_RIDER x7; the Andalusian host at Tours was overwhelmingly horse, and the engine's light/heavy cavalry would have been closer.
strengths: Correct date and place stated up front (October 732, between Tours and Poitiers) with no invented events.
Terrain is a densely wooded ridge (4,640 oak trees), matching the wooded high ground Martel chose.
Frankish force is infantry-heavy (militia, man-at-arms, spearmen, pikemen, champions), correctly modelling the shield wall, against an all-mounted Umayyad force.
Duke Odo's flanking strike on the Umayyad camp is scripted as a mid-battle event, matching the Mozarabic Chronicle's account of the raid that disordered the invaders.

Victory conditions encode the two historical outcomes precisely: the death of the emir, or the Aquitanians reaching the enemy camp forcing withdrawal; defeat is the fall of the Frankish leader or the shield wall being overrun.
Narration quotes the chronicle's 'wall, immovable as a block of ice' and ends with the overnight Umayyad withdrawal south rather than a rout.
justification: The scenario's structure, terrain, and scripting are unusually faithful: a wooded ridge, an infantry shield wall against all-cavalry attackers, Odo's camp raid as the turning point, and victory gated on Abd al-Rahman's death or the camp being taken — exactly the history's turning points and outcome. The casting, however, is badly avoidable: Charles Martel is WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR (1066), Abd al-Rahman is SALADIN (12th-century Ayyubid), and Duke Odo is EL_CID, so every named leader is from the wrong century and two from the wrong culture, when renamed generic units were available. Both players are also left on RANDOM civilization, leaving architecture and unit character unfixed despite Franks and a Saracen-type civ existing in the engine. The text itself asserts nothing false and even quotes the Mozarabic Chronicle correctly.

issues_found: Charles Martel is represented by WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR, a Norman duke of 1066 — over three centuries after 732 and a different polity; a renamed generic Champion/Militia hero-unit was the correct choice since the engine ships no Carolingian hero.
Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi is represented by SALADIN, a 12th-century Kurdish Ayyubid sultan — wrong century, wrong dynasty, wrong region.
Duke Odo of Aquitaine is represented by EL_CID, an 11th-century Castilian; wrong era and wrong side of the Pyrenees.

Both active players are set to RANDOM civilization, so architecture and unit graphics are unassigned — Franks and Saracens were the obvious available picks and the Umayyad player could easily have been Saracen.
CAMEL_RIDER x7 as the core of the Umayyad strike force; the army at Tours was Arab-Berber horse cavalry, and the engine's Knight/Light Cavalry (already partly used) covers it better than camels.
PIKEMAN x4 in the Frankish line is a 14th-15th century unit line; Spearman/Militia would suffice for 8th-century Frankish infantry.
Force scale is tiny (about 20 Franks against 21 Umayyad riders) on a 120x120 map, giving no sense of the dense shield-wall formation the narration emphasises.

Duke Odo's raid on the Umayyad camp is presented as a decisive scripted flank attack; the sources credit a Frankish raiding party on the camp only vaguely, so its attribution to Odo is an embellishment.
strengths: Date and place are correct: October 732, between Tours and Poitiers, on a wooded ridge — and 4,640 oak trees genuinely realise the forested high ground the Franks used to break cavalry momentum.

Victory on slaying the enemy emir matches the historical outcome — Abd al-Rahman was killed in the melee — and the alternate victory by reaching the enemy camp encodes the camp raid and nocturnal withdrawal.
Defeat conditions are the historically correct ones for the Frankish side: loss of Charles Martel, or enemy horsemen penetrating into the Frankish camp area (the wall being overrun).
Narration quotes the Mozarabic Chronicle's 'wall, immovable as a block of ice' and correctly ends with a night withdrawal southward rather than a pursuit or annihilation.

The casting, however, is badly anachronistic in an avoidable way: William the Conqueror stands in for Charles Martel, Saladin for Abd al-Rahman, and El Cid for Duke Odo, all from the wrong centuries, when renamed generic units were available. Leaving both players' civilizations RANDOM also forfeits the obvious Frankish and Saracen architecture sets, and camel riders misrepresent Arab-Berber horse. Text-level pedagogy is otherwise sound and even cites the chronicle simile accurately.

The narration attributes the second charge directly to news of the burning camp, a causal sequence the sources do not assert (the camp raid is generally placed at the crisis of the battle, not as a mid-battle provocation).
strengths: Force composition by type is correct: an all-infantry Frankish force (militia line, spearmen) versus an all-mounted Umayyad force (camel riders, cavalry archers, knights) plus a small cavalry-heavy Aquitanian third party.
4,640 oak trees create the wooded high ground the sources emphasise as the Frankish advantage against cavalry.

Victory condition on slaying the enemy commander matches Abd al-Rahman's actual death on the field; the alternative victory on getting Odo's men (player 3) into the enemy camp area encodes the historical raid on the Umayyad baggage train.
Defeat conditions — loss of the Frankish commander or ten enemy horsemen penetrating the Frankish position — encode exactly the risk the Franks faced (a broken line and an open road north).
The dusk stalemate and overnight Umayyad withdrawal southward is the historically attested outcome.
The 'like a wall, immovable as a block of ice' line is a genuine quotation from the Mozarabic Chronicle of 754, and the October 732 dating and Tours–Poitiers location are correct.
justification: The scenario's structure is unusually faithful: an infantry defence in woods, a three-way order of battle with Odo's Aquitanians raiding the baggage camp, and victory/defeat conditions keyed to the death of Abd al-Rahman, the raid on the camp, the survival of the Frankish commander, and the integrity of the line — precisely what the history turned on. The casting, however, is badly wrong in an avoidable way: William the Conqueror plays Charles Martel, Saladin plays Abd al-Rahman, and El Cid plays Duke Odo, three heroes drawn from the 11th and 12th centuries when renamed generic units were available. Both active players are left on RANDOM civilization, so the Frankish and Umayyad visual and unit identity is not actually guaranteed despite the correct infantry-versus-cavalry split. The in-game text is accurate on date, place, outcome, and even quotes the Mozarabic Chronicle correctly.

Only two players exist, so the Merkits, Jamukha's Jadaran and the Naiman confederation are all the same opponent. The dramatic core of the brief — an alliance forged and then broken — is reduced to a CHANGE_OWNERSHIP trigger rather than a real allied third party turning hostile.

Player 1's force is 11 cavalry archers plus a handful of villagers: a horse-archer warband with almost no infantry, which is exactly the composition the sources describe for a steppe nokod.

GAIA roster of 14 sheep, 4 deer, forage bushes and 15 rock formations reads as open pastoral steppe with herds — the correct economic and visual base.

The event sequence is the historical one and in the right order: Merkit raid and Borte's rescue, alliance with Jamukha, Jamukha's betrayal of the blood-oath (anda), destruction of the Naiman and death of Tayang Khan, then the 1206 kurultai and the title Genghis Khan.
The narration names Borte, Jamukha, Tayang Khan and the kurultai correctly and translates 'Genghis Khan' as 'Ruler of All Peoples' — accurate and instructive.
Defeat is keyed to the death of Temujin himself, which correctly encodes the fact that the confederation was personal and would have scattered without him — the text even says so.

The encoded goal — kill the enemy leader, lose if Temujin dies — is close to the history's own logic, and the narration asserts little that the sources do not.

Defeat is gated on the death of Temujin himself, correctly reflecting that the coalition was personal and would have dissolved with him — the narration says exactly this.

Sheep, deer, and open pasture support a pastoral-economy reading of the map.
justification: The narration and trigger sequence track the Secret History's outline closely — Borte's abduction and extraction, the blood-oath with Jamukha and its rupture, Tayang Khan's death, and the 1206 kurultai — and the all-cavalry rosters plus yurt encampments read convincingly as steppe. The weaknesses are avoidable engine choices: both civilizations are left RANDOM when Mongols exist, Tayang Khan is embodied by the European KING model, Jamukha exists only as a line of dialogue and an ownership change, and Toghrul of the Kereit, who actually retrieved Borte, is missing entirely. Victory on Tayang Khan and defeat on Temujin encode a recognisably historical goal, though the unification the brief promises is reduced to a single assassination.

title: The Siege of Vienna

issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so architecture, unit bonuses and visual identity for the Habsburg garrison and the Ottoman army are left to chance — the engine offers Turks (with Janissaries and bombards) and Teutons/Spanish, so this was avoidable.
The text explicitly promises 'Spanish arquebusiers', yet the garrison's ranged arm is CROSSBOWMAN x6 and SKIRMISHER x4; the engine ships HAND_CANNONEER, the obvious 1529 gunpowder stand-in.

The Ottoman assault force is CROSSBOWMAN x6 with no gunpowder infantry — the Janissary corps, the single most characteristic element of Suleiman's army, has no representative (JANISSARY/HAND_CANNONEER exists in the engine).

Ottoman order of battle is cavalry-heavy (CAMEL_RIDER x5, LIGHT_CAVALRY x4, CAVALRY_ARCHER x6) for an operation that was fought as trench, mine and infantry assault work against a walled city; akinci raiders were used for foraging, not for storming the Carinthian Gate.
BOMBARD_CANNON and ONAGER overstate Ottoman firepower: Suleiman's heavy siege guns were bogged down and largely left behind on the Danube march, which is precisely why the Ottomans relied on mining.

Both commanders are represented by the generic KING object; acceptable as a renamed stand-in, but a KING is an odd cast for a city defence commander and for a Sultan in camp, and no attempt is made at a culturally appropriate hero unit.
3541 oak trees dominate the map; the Vienna glacis had in fact been cleared of cover and suburbs burned before the siege, so heavy forest right up to the works is misleading.
Salm's death as an instant-defeat condition slightly misstates history — Salm was mortally wounded during the siege yet Vienna held.
strengths: The defence is correctly built around pike-and-shot infantry (PIKEMAN, CHAMPION) behind a substantial STONE_WALL x123 circuit with CASTLE, KEEP and GUARD_TOWERs, matching the Landsknecht garrison behind Vienna's medieval curtain.
The Ottoman side is staged as a besieging camp (PAVILION_C, TENT_D/E, BONFIRE, SIEGE_WORKSHOP, BATTERING_RAM) rather than a rival town, which is the right shape for a siege.

The mining sequence is modelled explicitly: 'Sappers Detected' warning, a KILL_OBJECT detonation that opens a breach, spawned raiders, and a 'Repel the Sappers' resolution — the actual decisive mechanism of the 1529 siege.
Three escalating assault waves followed by the autumn rains, supply failure and the 14 October withdrawal reproduce the correct chronology and outcome.

Victory is gated on a timer plus holding an area, and defeat on the Town Center or the commander — encoding 'outlast the Sultan', exactly the problem Salm faced, rather than a generic annihilation goal.
Incidental detail is well chosen: the ROMAN_RUINS nod to Vindobona, and the St Stephen's Cathedral bells dialogue.
justification: The scenario gets the strategic problem right — a walled garrison of pikes and towers that must survive mining, three assaults and a timer, with defeat on the Town Center or Salm, which is precisely the historical 'hold until the rains' objective. It is undermined by execution details that were avoidable in this engine: both players are RANDOM civilization, the promised Spanish arquebusiers appear as crossbowmen and skirmishers, and the Ottoman storming parties contain no Janissary or gunpowder infantry at all while fielding camels and light cavalry against a curtain wall. Narration and event sequencing are accurate and dated correctly (mine, breach, October rains, 14 October withdrawal), so the text teaches well even where the placed roster contradicts it.

justification: The tactical skeleton is sound: a wooded ridge of nearly 6,000 trees, a Frankish infantry block of spearmen and militia against an all-cavalry Umayyad force, an Odo flanking trigger against the camp, and victory gated on killing the enemy commander or outlasting ten minutes — all of which match the shape and outcome of Tours. The casting, however, is indefensible: Charles Martel is William the Conqueror, Abd al-Rahman is Saladin, and Duke Odo is El Cid, three heroes from three wrong centuries and, in two cases, wrong cultures, when renamed generic units would have been correct. Leaving both players on RANDOM civilization compounds this, since the Umayyad camp's castle, walls and towers may render in any architecture the engine picks. The narration and objectives themselves are accurate and would teach an attentive player the right story, but the placed content repeatedly contradicts them.

Escalating wave sizes (15, 24, 31, 43 spawned units) with an announced 'full strength' final assault mirrors the pattern of probing attacks culminating in one great assault.

Primary victory is a 600-second survival timer, which is the correct shape of objective for a defensive siege the defenders needed only to outlast, and defeat is keyed to the loss of the defenders' central stronghold rather than to enemy survival.
justification: The objective encoding is sound — outlast a deadline, lose if the central stronghold falls — and the stone-wall circuit with sealed gates is a reasonable abstraction of the Theodosian defences. Everything identifying the combatants, however, is wrong in an avoidable way: Richard the Lionheart plays Constantine XI and Saladin plays Mehmed II, both figures of the 1180s from unrelated polities, both civilizations are left RANDOM, and the siege's defining instrument, Ottoman bombard artillery, appears nowhere among the 223 placed objects. The setting adds palm forest to the Bosphorus and omits the Golden Horn and sea walls the brief promises, while the narration ends by asserting the Ottoman assault broke — the opposite of what happened on 29 May 1453.

Defender roster of crossbowmen, men-at-arms and militia-grade villagers behind stone walls, guard towers and a castle is a fair abstraction of the ~7,000 Greek and Genoese defenders manning the land walls.
Massive asymmetry of numbers is encoded structurally: four escalating assault waves of 15, 24, 31 and 43 spawned units against a fixed garrison of 17 combatants.
Defeat is keyed to the loss of the player's own core structures (Castle, Town Center), not to attrition, which matches a defender who loses by losing the city.
Primary victory is a 600-second survival timer — the correct shape of goal for a siege the defenders needed only to outlast.
Difficulty triggers scale the besieging force rather than the defenders, preserving the asymmetric siege framing.
justification: The text layer is well-researched — 1453, Mehmed II, Constantine XI, the Theodosian Walls, escalating assaults against a thin garrison — and the encoded conditions correctly make survival to a deadline the win and the loss of the city's core the defeat. But the placed content contradicts the text at the two most visible points: the defender of Byzantium is Richard the Lionheart and the Sultan is Saladin, two Third Crusade figures three centuries and two cultures displaced, and both civilizations are left RANDOM so no Byzantine or Turkish identity is guaranteed. Setting further slips with palm forests on the Bosphorus, while the brief's promised Golden Horn sea walls and bombard breaches have no objects behind them at all — no ships, no docks, no siege train. The generic 'eliminate all player 2 units' alternate victory path also dilutes an otherwise correctly-framed outlast objective.

No English or Burgundian commander of any kind is placed or named; the opposing force is an anonymous wall-and-castle garrison.

Troyes historically capitulated after negotiation and the threat of assault (Chalons opened its gates outright); the scenario's only Troyes outcome is 'The gates of Troyes have fallen!' via a DESTROY_OBJECT trigger on the gate, contradicting the brief's own claim that garrisons could be 'persuaded to surrender'.

The 'Ambush at the river crossing' near Chalons and the two timed 'Pursuit Wave' cavalry sorties from Troyes are inventions — no English field pursuit or river-crossing battle occurred on the march to Reims.
The Player 3 'raider chief' side quest (CHAMPION + MILITIA x5) rewarding six allied PIKEMEN is a wholly fictional episode inserted into a documented march.
Victory is triggered by JOAN_OF_ARC entering the Reims area, not by the KING (Dauphin Charles), even though the brief and history make the Dauphin's arrival the point of the campaign.
2,880 oak trees dominate a 120x120 map representing the open chalk plains of Champagne.
strengths: JOAN_OF_ARC is the correct engine hero for the correct person, campaign, and year.
The Dauphin is represented by the KING unit, an apt engine stand-in for an uncrowned monarch who must survive.
Defeat on the death of the KING encodes the real stake: without Charles there is no coronation.
The route's actual obstacles — Troyes and Chalons — are named and placed in sequence between the start and Reims.
A MONASTERY stands in for Reims Cathedral, a reasonable substitution given the engine has no cathedral.
Narration correctly dates the march to June 1429, places it after Orleans, and names the outcome as Charles VII's coronation.
justification: The scenario gets the principals right — the real Joan of Arc hero escorting a KING-unit Dauphin past Troyes and Chalons to a monastery-as-cathedral at Reims — and correctly makes the Dauphin's death a defeat. But both players are left on RANDOM civilization, so the architecture and troops of an English-held Champagne are unspecified, and the garrison is crossbowmen and pikemen rather than the available Briton longbowmen. Historically Troyes negotiated its surrender and Chalons simply opened its gates; here the only path is smashing the Troyes gate, plus an invented river ambush, two invented cavalry pursuits, and a fictional raider-chief quest. Victory also fires on Joan reaching Reims rather than on the Dauphin, the person the coronation actually required.

'The garrison prepares for a fair fight' and the alternate 'eliminate all player 2 objects' victory path both cut against a siege in which a heavily outnumbered garrison simply had to endure.
Wave spawn triggers create forces for a player whose only placed object is Saladin, so the besieging army has no historically flavoured standing presence (no Janissary/Hand Cannoneer garrison camp).
strengths: The primary victory condition is a survival timer with defeat on loss of the Castle/Town Center, which correctly encodes a siege the defenders needed only to outlast rather than win by counter-attack.

Narration names the correct principals and date — September 1529, Suleiman, Niklas Graf Salm — and the closing dialogue invokes the autumn rains that actually ended the siege.
An optional objective to slay the enemy commander is kept subordinate to the survival requirement, matching the fact that killing the Sultan was never the defenders' path to success.
justification: The scenario's framing text knows the history — 1529, Suleiman, Salm, the Carinthian Gate, the autumn rains — but nothing placed on the map supports it: the Ottoman army is one SALADIN hero from the wrong culture and the wrong century, the defenders are generic Crossbowmen and Men-at-Arms rather than the available Landsknechts and Hand Cannoneers, and both civilizations are left RANDOM so the architecture is arbitrary. The setting is a 6,667-tree forest with no siege camp and no countermining, and the four escalating waves are a generic tower-defence rhythm rather than the mine-and-breach assaults on the Kärntnertor. The one strong element is the encoded goal: survive 600 seconds or lose the Castle, which is the right shape for a siege the garrison had only to outlast, even though the accompanying text mislabels a three-week siege as a night's vigil.

title: Marco Polo on the Silk Road
objective_facts:

issues_found: Marco Polo is represented by the EL_CID hero — an 11th-century Castilian mounted warlord, wrong culture and wrong century, and avoidable since the editor permits renaming a generic villager, trade cart or monk to stand in for a Venetian merchant.
Niccolo Polo is represented by FREDERICK_BARBAROSSA, a 12th-century Holy Roman Emperor; again an unrelated figure where a renamed generic unit was available.

Kublai Khan is never placed. The destination is only a GAIA TOWN_CENTER with two yurts and flags; the Khan whose court is the whole point of the journey has no representation at all (Genghis Khan hero or a renamed cavalry/monk unit could have served).

Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so the caravan and the Central Asian raiders may render in any architecture (Teutonic, Japanese, Meso-American), undermining an explicitly Silk Road setting.

The escort force is a Western European retinue — knights, crossbowmen, spearmen — whereas the Polos travelled as a small merchant party with hired local guides and Mongol safe-conduct (paiza), not an armed column.
Maffeo Polo, Niccolo's brother and a member of the actual 1271 journey, is absent.
Palm forest as the dominant vegetation across a map that is supposed to include the Pamirs and Gobi is a poor fit for the high passes.

The two bandit ambushes are invented set pieces; the historical hazards on this leg were principally the Karaunas brigands in Persia, disease (Marco's long illness in Badakhshan) and altitude/desert attrition, none of which are modelled.
strengths: Player 2's roster — cavalry archers, light cavalry, scout cavalry and a yurt encampment — is a fitting representation of mounted Central Asian raiders.

Narration is factually sound on dates and details: 1271 departure from Venice, Marco aged seventeen, the Pamirs as 'the Roof of the World', roughly four years en route, and seventeen years subsequently in Kublai's service.
Victory is gated on bringing the Marco Polo unit to the Shangdu area rather than on destroying the enemy, which is exactly the historical objective of a caravan journey.
Defeat on the death of Marco and on the loss of all pack animals (sheep) encodes the two real risks to the expedition — the man and the goods.
Terrain furniture (cliffs, rock formations, gold and stone mines, bonfires, yurts, tents and pavilion) gives a recognisable caravan-and-encampment progression across the route.
Trigger sequence stages the journey: first ambush, mountain pass crossing with a resource change, second ambush, approach to Shangdu — a coherent west-to-east arc.
justification: The scenario's structure and text are genuinely good history — the 1271 departure, Marco's age, the Pamir crossing, the 1275 arrival at Shangdu and the seventeen years at court are all correct, and the victory condition (deliver Marco to Shangdu) with defeat on his death or the loss of the pack animals is precisely the goal the sources pose. The casting, however, is badly wrong in an avoidable way: Marco Polo is EL_CID and Niccolo is FREDERICK_BARBAROSSA, two figures from the wrong cultures and the wrong centuries, when renamed generic units were available; Kublai Khan, the object of the journey, is not placed at all, and Maffeo Polo is missing. Both civilizations are left RANDOM, so the architecture of the caravan and of the Mongol camp is unspecified, and the escort is a European knight-and-crossbow retinue rather than a merchant party. The invented pair of dune ambushes substitutes for the documented perils of Persian brigands, illness and altitude, but preserves the broad shape of a threatened overland crossing.

20 TREE_PALM_FOREST tiles carry the whole landscape, including the Pamir 'Roof of the World' leg, where palms are botanically absurd; cliffs and rock formations alone carry the mountain passage.

Leaving both civilizations RANDOM and dressing Constantinople in palm forest squanders the engine's Byzantine and Turkish rosters. Most damagingly, victory is encoded as slaying the besieging sultan, which is neither what the defenders could do nor what happened; the historical condition was to outlast the assault, and the closing text asserting that the walls held is a counterfactual the sources do not support.

issues_found: Both the Merkit chieftain and Tayang Khan of the Naiman are represented by the generic KING unit — a crowned European monarch model, culturally wrong for steppe tribal leaders. The engine ships mounted steppe-era heroes (e.g. Kushluk, historically Tayang Khan's own son; Subotai) that would have been far closer, so this is avoidable.

Jamukha, named repeatedly in the narration as blood-brother, ally, and then betrayer, is never placed or created as a unit — his 'betrayal' is only a spawn of anonymous CAVALRY_ARCHER/LIGHT_CAVALRY. The scenario's central relationship has no on-map embodiment.

Toghrul/Wang Khan and the Kereit confederation, indispensable to Temujin's rise (and to the actual Borte rescue and the later war that preceded the Naiman campaign), are entirely absent — only two players are active.

Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so architecture, unit skins, and tech could render as Teutonic, Britons, or anything else; Mongols was available and should have been assigned to at least Player 1.
CAMEL_RIDER x3 in the Naiman roster is wrong: the Naiman were a Turkic-Mongol steppe horse-archer confederation, and the AoE2 camel rider is a Middle Eastern unit with no place on the Altai steppe.

The Naiman camp is defined by PALISADE_WALL x10, a GATE and two GUARD_TOWERs — a sedentary fortified enclosure, whereas Tayang Khan's host was a mobile nomadic camp (the yurts placed alongside are correct; the masonry towers are not).

The chronology of the Borte rescue is inverted: historically Temujin recovered Borte from the Merkits *with* Jamukha's and Toghrul's armies; here the Jamukha alliance is triggered only after the Merkit chieftain is already dead.
Only 106 objects on a 120x120 map means the 'unification of the tribes' is fought against a single enemy camp; the plurality of tribes (Tatars, Kereits, Taichiud) the brief promises is unrepresented.
strengths: GENGHIS_KHAN is the correct engine hero for Temujin and is placed as the player's leader with defeat gated on his death — appropriate for a warband leader whose loss would scatter his followers.
Player 1's roster (CAVALRY_ARCHER, LIGHT_CAVALRY, SCOUT_CAVALRY, no infantry, a Stable and Archery Range) is a faithful abstraction of a mounted steppe warband.
YURT_A through YURT_D used for both camps instead of stone housing is the right architectural choice for the steppe.
GAIA placement of SHEEP x6, WILD_BOAR x4, FORAGE_BUSH and ROCK_FORMATION_1 x15 evokes a pastoral, rocky steppe rather than farmland.
Victory on killing Tayang Khan is the genuine turning point: his death at Chakirmaut in 1204 broke the Naiman and cleared the path to the 1206 kurultai.
The narration's dates (1186 opening, 1206 kurultai on the Onon, the title 'Universal Ruler') are correct and specific.
justification: The scenario gets the arc right — Merkit feud, Jamukha alliance and betrayal, Naiman war, kurultai of 1206 — and encodes victory on the death of Tayang Khan and defeat on Temujin's, which is the historical stake rather than a generic annihilation. But the execution undercuts it: both antagonist chieftains are the crowned European KING unit when steppe cavalry heroes were available, Jamukha exists only in text, Toghrul and the Kereits are absent, camel riders and a palisade-and-guard-tower fort intrude on the steppe, and leaving both players on RANDOM civilization forfeits the one setting choice that was free. The Borte rescue is also decoupled from the allies who actually made it possible.

The 'Find Allies / Allies Join' caravan-guard side quest reflects the real practice of caravans hiring local escorts against bandits.
justification: The objective layer is genuinely historical — victory turns on delivering one named traveller to Shangdu and defeat on his death, exactly the stake the Polos faced — and the waypoint triggers correctly model a journey rather than a battle. But the cast is badly wrong: Marco Polo is played by Richard the Lionheart, an English king dead seventy years before the journey began, Kublai Khan and Maffeo Polo are absent entirely, Shangdu is an empty map region with no palace, and the pack animals the brief makes central are simply not placed. Both players are left on RANDOM civilization, so the architecture is unspecified, and the bandits are led by a Norse BERSERK while the Mongols are recast as treacherous ambushers against the sources.

The narrative asserts that 'the riders of the Khan were waiting in the rocks' and that a Mongol camp bars the pass. Historically the Polos travelled under Kublai's protection with a golden passport tablet; Mongol authority secured the road rather than ambushing them. This is invented and actively misleading.
The four-year, multi-thousand-mile journey (Acre, Hormuz, Pamirs, Taklamakan, Gansu) is compressed into a single 80x80 palm-fringed desert with no distinguishable stages beyond generic waypoint text.

The scenario is structured as a movement/escort mission with sequential BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA waypoints rather than a battle of annihilation, which matches the shape of a journey.
Victory is gated on the protagonist reaching a specific destination area and defeat on his death — the correct kind of condition for an escort across Asia.
Terrain dressing (palm forest, rock formations, cliffs, gold and stone mines, an oasis midpoint) evokes desert and mountain-pass travel.
justification: The encoded objective is sound — bring the protagonist alive to a fixed destination, lose if he dies — which is exactly what the 1271-1275 journey posed. Almost everything else is miscast: Marco Polo is played by Richard the Lionheart, a hero from the wrong culture and a century too early; his 'caravan' is knights and crossbowmen with not a single trade cart or pack animal despite the brief; the bandit chief is a Viking Berserk; Kublai Khan and any building representing Shangdu are absent; and both civilizations are left RANDOM so the architecture is undefined. Norman roster combines KNIGHT, ARCHER and MAN_AT_ARMS, matching the combined-arms assault the sources describe.
Primary victory condition is DESTROY_OBJECT on Harold (the KING), the actual turning point that ended the battle and the Anglo-Saxon monarchy.
Defeat on William's death echoes the real crisis when rumour of his fall nearly broke the Norman line and he had to bare his head to rally them.
Narration correctly dates the battle to 14 October 1066, names Senlac Hill, and distinguishes huscarls at the centre from fyrd on the flanks.
justification: The combatant side is handled well: William is the correct named hero, Harold is a properly substituted generic KING, and the Saxon force is deliberately all-infantry against a Norman knight/archer/infantry mix. The setting is the weak point — both civilizations are left RANDOM, and the Saxons are given a Castle, 29 wall segments and guard towers on a ridge where Harold in fact had no fortification at all, while 4,800 oaks bury the open downland the narration describes. The encoded goal is largely right (kill Harold, keep William alive), though the 900-second automatic Norman victory misreads a nightfall that would have favoured the defenders, and the celebrated feigned retreat is asserted in dialogue but never implemented in triggers.

The actual turning points — the victory over Aragon and Berenguer Ramon II at Almenar/Tevar, the capture of the Cid's Castilian rival, the 1094 siege and taking of Valencia, and the defence at Cuarte in 1094 — are absent.
Valencia, the stated culmination of the brief, is never named in the in-game text or encoded in any condition; the final target is an anonymous 'enemy stronghold'.

Defeat is also triggered by the death of Player 3's KING (Al-Mutamin). Al-Mutamin died naturally in 1085 and his death did not end El Cid's career; the Cid simply continued serving his son al-Musta'in.
Victory on destroying a single GATE_NORTH_TO_SOUTH inside an area is an engine bookkeeping condition, not the historical goal of taking and holding a city.
strengths: EL_CID, the correct engine hero for Rodrigo Diaz de Vivar, is the player's protagonist and his death is the defeat condition, matching the brief's 'losing El Cid himself means defeat'.
The opening narration correctly dates the exile to 1081, names King Alfonso VI of Castile as the man who banished him, and identifies the taifa of Zaragoza as his first employer.

justification: The scenario gets its protagonist right — El Cid himself, with his death as the defeat trigger — and its framing text correctly names Alfonso VI, the 1081 exile, and Al-Mutamin of Zaragoza. The narrative replaces Almenar, Tevar and the 1094 conquest of Valencia — never named anywhere — with generic 'Ambusher', 'Traitor King' and 'Rescued Ally' beats, and victory reduces to killing the enemy hero or knocking down a gate, a default that would fit any period engagement, though the El Cid defeat condition is faithful to the brief.

issues_found: Both players are set to RANDOM civilization, so Norman and Anglo-Saxon architecture, unit bonuses and visual identity are left to chance — Franks/Britons were available and avoidable error.

4,800 TREE_OAK objects blanket a 120x120 map; Senlac Hill was an open ridge with a marshy bottom and cleared slopes, not dense forest, and heavy woods make the cavalry-versus-shield-wall action the brief describes impossible to stage.

Random-map economic furniture (10 gold mines, 8 stone mines, 16 forage bushes, 12 sheep, 8 deer) plus Town Centers, Blacksmith, Archery Range, Stable, Barracks and Monastery frame a base-building match rather than a single-day pitched battle; no army in 1066 was building a monastery on the field.
Player 2 receives 2 Guard Towers, and both sides a Town Center — no fortifications existed on Senlac Hill; Harold's strength was the unfortified shield wall itself.
Harold is represented by the KING unit, a militarily inert object, whereas Harold fought and died in the line; a renamed Champion or Teutonic Knight would have been a truer stand-in.

The 'Feigned Retreat Draws the Housecarls' trigger only prints text — no housecarls actually break formation or change ownership/stance, so the battle's decisive tactic is asserted rather than modelled.
strengths: WILLIAM_THE_CONQUEROR is the engine's correct hero for the Norman commander, and Harold Godwinson is properly renamed onto a generic unit since no Harold hero ships with the game.

Force composition matches the sources: Normans get combined Knights (20), Archers (14) and Man-at-Arms (10); the Anglo-Saxons get Champions (housecarls) and Spearmen with almost no archers (4) and, correctly, no cavalry at all.
Victory is gated on killing Harold specifically, and defeat on either William's death or a 1500-second nightfall deadline with Harold still alive — precisely the two-sided problem of 14 October 1066.

Narration is accurate and correctly dated (October 14th, 1066; Senlac Hill; the road to London; the 'Out! Out!' war cry) and correctly identifies the feigned retreat as the mechanism that thinned the wall.
Sequenced triggers (reaching the ridge, the feint, dusk approaching) reproduce the chronological shape of the engagement.
justification: The scenario's framing is unusually faithful: William is the correct shipped hero, Harold is a renamed generic unit as the rubric prescribes, the rosters correctly give the Normans cavalry-and-archer combined arms and the Saxons an all-infantry wall with no horse, and the win/lose conditions encode exactly the historical problem — kill Harold before nightfall, and lose if William falls or dusk comes with the wall intact. The setting, however, undermines all of it: both civilizations are left RANDOM, and 4,800 oak trees plus ten gold mines, stone mines, sheep, and a full complement of production buildings and Guard Towers turn the open ridge at Senlac into a forested random map with two bases. The feigned retreat, the battle's turning point, is only narrated by a DISPLAY_INSTRUCTIONS trigger rather than mechanically enacted, though the sequence of events and all in-game text are historically sound and correctly dated.

issues_found: Both players are assigned RANDOM civilization, so Byzantine and Turkish architecture, unit rosters and bonuses (both of which the engine ships) are left to chance — the single most avoidable error here.

justification: The trigger design is the strongest part of this scenario: defeat on the Hagia Sophia object and victory on simply surviving encode exactly the goal Constantine faced, and the scripted beats (St. Romanus breach, the Golden Horn probe, Giustiniani's wounding, the 29 May general assault) follow the sources in order. The placed content undercuts the text, however: both civilizations are RANDOM when Byzantines and Turks are both in the game, the promised Janissaries are MAN_AT_ARMS, and the sea-wall assault on the Golden Horn happens on a map with no water and no ships at all. Palm forest on the Bosphorus and a mere 49 wall tiles standing in for the Theodosian double wall compound an otherwise well-narrated siege.

justification: The scenario gets the frame right: Joan's own hero unit escorts a renamed KING, and the encoded victory (King reaches the Reims cathedral area) and defeat (King slain) are exactly the historical stakes of the 1429 march, not a generic kill-the-enemy default. It falters on the substance of the campaign: Champagne's garrisons were Anglo-Burgundian, and Troyes capitulated by negotiation while Chalons simply opened its gates, yet the only implemented progression triggers are DESTROY_OBJECT on both towns, so play teaches two storms that never occurred despite the brief advertising a surrender path. issues_found: Maffeo Polo, Niccolo's brother who accompanied the 1271 journey and had already made the first trip to Kublai's court, is entirely absent; a second renamed villager would have cost nothing.

Kublai Khan himself is never placed or named at Shangdu; the destination is an empty GAIA Castle/Town Center cluster, so the player never meets the figure the whole journey is about.

A European CASTLE stands in for the Khan's summer palace at Shangdu; the PAVILION_A used in the Polo camp would have been a more apt Asiatic structure for the imperial site.
strengths: Player 1 correctly assigned ITALIANS for the Venetian Polos and Player 2 MONGOLS for the steppe raiders — the right two cultures, not generic filler.

Victory is gated on the death of Tayang Khan, the Naiman leader whose defeat at Chakirmaut in 1204 cleared the way for the 1206 kurultai, and defeat on the loss of Temujin himself — both the historically decisive stakes.
The closing text correctly places the kurultai and the proclamation as Genghis Khan in 1206.
justification: The scenario gets the medium's hardest parts right: the correct Mongol protagonist using the engine's Genghis Khan hero, an all-cavalry steppe roster, yurt encampments and steppe fauna, and a victory condition tied to the specific death (Tayang Khan) that actually preceded the 1206 kurultai, with defeat on Temujin's own fall. The weaknesses are in the history itself: Toghrul/Wang Khan and the Kereit are missing from a Borte rescue they largely conducted, the Jamukha alliance is placed after rather than before that rescue, and the text kills Toghtoa Beki, who in fact escaped. Assigning the enemy TURKS when Mongols was available, and dressing chieftains as a Knight and a Cavalier, are avoidable roster errors.

title: The Road to Reims
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on KING reaching area (105,57)-(111,63) [path "[VC] Coronation at Reims"]
Defeat:
  - DESTROY_OBJECT on KING (player 1) [path "[Defeat] The Dauphin Falls"]
issues_found: The garrisons of Troyes and Chalons are cast purely as Britons/English; in fact both towns were Anglo-Burgundian, with Burgundian loyalties the decisive factor in their surrender. No Burgundian presence or distinction is represented despite the engine offering additional players/civilizations.

No French commanders other than Joan appear: the Duke of Alençon, the Bastard of Orleans (Dunois) and La Trémoïlle all rode with the column, and the engine ships suitable hero/renamed-unit options for at least some of them.

The march east is preceded in the sources by the Loire campaign and the field victory at Patay (18 June 1429); the narration jumps straight from 'the relief of Orleans' to the road to Reims, silently omitting the campaign that made the march possible.
Auxerre, the first town on the route to be passed by negotiation, is absent; only Troyes and Chalons are modelled.

The escort force of roughly 22 units badly understates the ~12,000-strong army that accompanied Charles, and there is no baggage/artillery representation of the siege train Joan drew up before Troyes.

The Troyes surrender text ('open the gates rather than face siege') and the 'Chalons submits without a blow, just as Troyes did before it' line flatten the fact that Troyes held out for days and only yielded after Joan visibly prepared an assault.
strengths: The engine's own Joan of Arc hero is used for Joan, the correct person, culture and year.
The Dauphin is a KING object renamed via CHANGE_OBJECT_NAME - exactly the right substitution for a figure the engine ships no hero for - and the Monastery is renamed as Reims Cathedral.

Franks for the royal army and Britons for the English garrisons are era- and place-appropriate civilization assignments, with Frankish knights/men-at-arms plus crossbowmen and pikemen a plausible 1429 composition.
Victory is BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA on the King at the Reims cathedral tile and defeat is DESTROY_OBJECT on the King - the encoded goal is precisely the historical one: get Charles to his crowning alive.

Both towns are built as walled, gated, castle-and-tower positions that can be bypassed, and the surrender triggers KILL_OBJECT the gates rather than requiring their destruction, mirroring the historical bloodless capitulations.
Dates are correct: June 1429 departure and the 17 July 1429 coronation of Charles VII.
justification: The scenario gets the essentials right: the correct Joan of Arc hero, a renamed KING standing in for the Dauphin, and a victory condition that is literally 'bring Charles to Reims cathedral alive' with defeat on his death - the historical goal rather than a generic annihilation. Troyes and Chalons are built as walled positions whose gates are removed by surrender triggers rather than requiring destruction, faithfully reproducing the two bloodless capitulations, and the 17 July coronation date is correct. The main avoidable faults are the flat 'English' casting of what were Anglo-Burgundian garrisons, the absence of Alençon and Dunois from a column that historically included them, and the silent omission of Patay and Auxerre between Orleans and Reims.

issues_found: The garrisons of Troyes and Chalons are labelled and modelled as purely English (Britons); in fact Champagne's towns in 1429 held Anglo-Burgundian allegiance, the Troyes garrison being a mixed force with Burgundian townsmen and a small English/Burgundian company. A third player set to Burgundians (or at least text acknowledging them) was available and avoidable error.
Auxerre, the first town on the march that negotiated passage and provisions before Troyes, is entirely absent, so the sequence of submissions is truncated.

No other French commanders of the march are represented: the Duke of Alencon, Dunois, La Hire and La Tremoille could all have been rendered as renamed Knights or Cavaliers, leaving the royal column with only Joan and the King as identifiable figures.

The [Ambush] Troyes Sortie and Chalons Sortie triggers invent armed sallies by garrisons that in fact never fought the royal army - both towns opened their gates without a blow, as the scenario's own narration states.
900 oak trees across a 120x120 map renders Champagne as dense forest rather than the open chalk plains and cultivated country the army actually crossed.

Player 1's force of 6 Knights, 6 Men-at-Arms, 5 Crossbowmen and 4 Pikemen is a very thin abstraction of a column reported at ten to twelve thousand; more of the same units were affordable within the object budget.
strengths: Joan of Arc is placed using the engine's actual Joan of Arc hero, the correct figure for June-July 1429, and the Dauphin is a KING unit renamed by trigger - the right solution for a figure with no hero model.
Franks for the French royal army and Britons for the English garrisons are the appropriate civilisation assignments in this engine.
The two barrier towns are correctly named and correctly ordered along the route: Troyes first, then Chalons, then Reims.
Both towns yield by BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA rather than by destruction, faithfully encoding that they opened their gates instead of being stormed.
The coronation date, 17 July 1429, and the title Charles VII are stated correctly.
Victory on the King entering the cathedral area and defeat on the King's death exactly reproduce the historical stake of the march.
justification: The scenario casts the correct engine hero for Joan, renames a KING for the Dauphin, and assigns Franks against Britons, with victory gated on the King physically reaching the Reims cathedral tile-area and defeat on his death - precisely the historical stake, not a generic annihilation goal. Its chief substantive error is treating Troyes and Chalons as straightforwardly English when they were Anglo-Burgundian towns, and omitting Auxerre from the chain of submissions; the two scripted garrison sorties also invent fighting that the narration itself denies took place. Terrain (900 oaks) forests over what should be open Champagne plain, and the escort column is skeletal, but the shape, sequence and outcome of the march to the coronation are recognisable and correctly dated.

Auxerre, which came to terms on the same march (early July 1429) and was the first town of the Champagne route to treat with the royal column, is absent from the road entirely.

The French column has no named captains besides Joan, although the engine ships period-correct French heroes from the Joan of Arc campaign (La Hire, Duke D'Alencon, Jean de Lorraine, Constable Richemont) who accompanied the historical march to Reims.
Player 2 fields 3 Cavalier alongside 3 Knight; a small-town garrison of 1429 would be foot soldiers, archers and a handful of men-at-arms, not two grades of heavy cavalry.
The 'Troyes Sortie' and 'Chalons Sortie' PATROL ambushes are invented; neither town sortied against the royal army.
strengths: Joan of Arc is placed as the engine's own JOAN_OF_ARC hero rather than a substitute, and the Dauphin is a KING object renamed 'Dauphin Charles' - the correct handling for a figure with no dedicated hero.
Civilizations are explicitly assigned and correct: Franks for the French royal column, Britons for the English-aligned garrisons.
Reims Cathedral is represented by a GAIA MONASTERY renamed via trigger, the closest ecclesiastical building the engine offers.
Victory is gated on the King reaching the cathedral tile area and defeat on his death - exactly the historical stake, since the march existed solely to deliver Charles to his anointing.
The coronation date, 17 July 1429, and the title 'King Charles VII' are stated correctly.
Both garrisons yield rather than being required to be destroyed, mirroring the bloodless opening of the Champagne road; the objective text explicitly permits pressing past them.
justification: The scenario gets the essentials right: the correct hero for Joan, a renamed KING for the Dauphin, Franks against Britons, and a victory condition that turns on the one thing the 1429 march was for - getting Charles alive to the cathedral at Reims, with his death as the defeat. Events follow the real sequence of Troyes then Chalons then Reims, and the coronation date is accurate. Marks come off for calling the Anglo-Burgundian garrisons simply 'English', for flattening Troyes' five-day blockade and threatened assault into a bloodless submission, for omitting Auxerre, and for leaving out the period-correct French captain heroes the engine already provides.

title: The Siege of Vienna
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS
(taken directly from the trigger graph; score `objective` from
these, not from the objectives text)

Victory:
  - TIMER on 300s elapsed [path "VC - Siege Lifted"]
Defeat:
  - OBJECTS_IN_AREA on count 3, player 2, area (40,60)-(55,75) [path "Defeat - City Falls"]
issues_found: No Janissaries in the Ottoman order of battle: the Turks civilization ships the Janissary, the elite gunpowder infantry that actually led the assaults on the Carinthian Gate, yet Player 2's assault waves are Camel Riders, Light Cavalry and Cavalry Archers — a steppe/raiding force wholly unsuited to storming a breached curtain wall.

The garrison text promises 'Spanish arquebusiers' but the placed roster contains only Crossbowmen, Pikemen and Spearmen; Teutons have access to Hand Cannoneers, so the omission of any gunpowder defender is avoidable and directly contradicts the narration.

Only two Bombard Cannons plus Mangonels/Onagers represent the Ottoman siege train; the mangonel/onager choice is engine-appropriate but the 300-gun bombardment that reduced the medieval wall is under-represented at a scale of two guns.
No Danube (or any water) on a 144x144 map: Vienna's position on the Danube, the Ottoman bridging problem, and the flooded/muddy camp that ended the siege are geographically absent.
1,414 oak trees crowd the map, whereas the ground before Vienna was a deliberately cleared glacis — the suburbs were burned by the defenders precisely to deny cover.

Salm is a renamed Champion (acceptable substitution) but Suleiman is a KING unit, a passive non-combatant that reads as a throne-piece rather than a commander; a renamed cavalry hero would have served better.
Withdrawal dated 14 October; the final great assault fell on 14 October and the Ottoman army broke camp on 15-16 October, so the closing narration compresses the climax out of the scenario.
The city itself is six houses, a Town Center, Market and Monastery — far too thin for a defended imperial city of ~20,000 with a garrison of 17,000-20,000.
strengths: Civilizations are correctly and explicitly assigned: Teutons for the German Landsknecht garrison, Turks for Suleiman's army, giving period-correct Central European and Ottoman architecture sets.
192 Stone Walls with a single Gate and a Keep reproduce the shape of the problem: a medieval curtain wall with one contested gate (the Carinthian Gate), named by trigger.

The Ottoman camp is built as a camp — Pavilion, twelve Tents, Bonfire and Flag — rather than as a second economic base, which is exactly right for a besieger operating at the end of a long supply line.
The mine/countermine sequence is the historically decisive mechanic, and it branches: killing the sapper preserves the wall, while failure detonates the mine and spawns attackers through a breach.
Three dated assaults (29 September, 6 October, 11 October) with Salm wounded at the breach tracks the real sequence of Ottoman attempts and Salm's mortal wounding in mid-October.

Victory on a timer with defeat on three Ottoman units reaching the city centre encodes the actual strategic problem: the defenders had only to outlast the campaign season, not to defeat the Ottoman army.
justification: The scenario gets the frame right — Teutons behind 192 tiles of stone wall against Turks in a tented camp, a named Carinthian Gate, a countermining branch, and dated assaults culminating in the autumn rains — and its win conditions encode precisely the historical goal of outlasting the campaign season while defeat is the enemy reaching the city's heart. The serious avoidable failure is force composition: the Turks civilization ships Janissaries and the Teutons ship Hand Cannoneers, yet the assaults are carried by Camel Riders and Light Cavalry while the 'Spanish arquebusiers' of the narration are represented by Crossbowmen, so the gunpowder character of both 1529 armies is simply absent. Setting is otherwise sound apart from a missing Danube and 1,414 trees on ground that was historically cleared. A playthrough would leave an attentive player with a broadly true picture, marred by a compressed withdrawal date and text that promises troops the map does not contain.

title: The Siege of Vienna
objective_facts:
EXTRACTED VICTORY AND DEFEAT CONDITIONS

issues_found: The text explicitly names 'Spanish arquebusiers', but the garrison contains 8 CROSSBOWMEN and no gunpowder infantry. Teutons have access to the Hand Cannoneer in the engine, so representing arquebusiers with crossbows is an avoidable substitution.

The Ottoman army contains no infantry whatsoever in the placed roster - no Janissary (available to the Turks) and no melee foot troops. Assaults on the Carinthian Gate mounted by Camel Riders, Light Cavalry and Cavalry Archers misrepresents the Ottoman storming parties, which were led by Janissaries.

Onagers and Mangonels (torsion/stone-throwing engines) pad the Ottoman siege train alongside only two Bombard Cannon; the historical besiegers relied on light field guns and, above all, mining, since heavy siege artillery had been left behind on the march.

Salm is stated to be wounded on 11 October; he was in fact struck down during the final great assault of 14 October (dying of the wound the following spring). The '29 September first great assault' is also invented - the Ottomans only completed investment around 27 September and the serious assaults came between 9 and 14 October.

The map is dominated by 1,414 oak trees with generic gold/stone mines and forage bushes; there is no representation of the Danube or the Wien river, or of the suburbs Salm demolished before the siege.

Suleiman is represented by a renamed KING and appears to sit in camp rather than the Sultan's actual position well behind the lines; acceptable as a stand-in but the accompanying single VILLAGER_MALE 'sapper' is the only mining representation for what was a large-scale Ottoman engineering effort.
strengths: Correct belligerent civilizations explicitly assigned: TEUTONS for the German/Imperial garrison of Vienna and TURKS for Suleiman's army, giving appropriate architecture on both sides.
Landsknecht pike is properly represented by 8 PIKEMEN plus 4 SPEARMEN behind stone walls, a keep, guard towers and a single gate - a defensible reading of Vienna's medieval curtain.

The countermining duel is modelled as a real mechanic: a renamed VILLAGER_MALE sapper who must be killed before reaching the Carinthian Gate, with a BRING_OBJECT_TO_AREA failure branch that blows a breach and spawns attackers.
Ottoman camp is dressed with PAVILION_C, twelve tents, a bonfire and a flag, and Turkish BOMBARD_CANNON are present - period-appropriate for 1529.
Victory is a timer (outlast the siege) and defeat is Ottoman units penetrating the city centre - exactly the win/lose conditions the defenders faced.
Narration follows the correct sequence: arrival, mining under the Carinthian Gate, successive assaults, autumn rain and supply exhaustion, withdrawal on 14 October 1529.
justification: The scenario gets the structural essentials right: Teutons versus Turks, a walled Vienna with pike-heavy garrison, a renamed villager as the Ottoman sapper whose mine must be countermined, a Turkish camp with bombard cannon, and a victory condition that correctly encodes 'hold until the besiegers leave' rather than destroying the Ottoman army. The defects are in composition and detail: the promised Spanish arquebusiers are 8 crossbowmen when Teutonic Hand Cannoneers were available, the Ottoman assault waves contain no infantry at all and notably no Janissaries, and the siege train is padded with Onagers and Mangonels. Dates are slightly invented - a 'first great assault' on 29 September and Salm wounded on 11 rather than 14 October - but the overall arc, including the mine-driven breach beside the Carinthian Gate and the rain-and-supply withdrawal of 14 October, is faithful.

title: The Siege of Vienna
objective_facts:

issues_found: The Ottoman roster contains no Janissaries and in fact no infantry at all - the engine's Turks ship the Janissary, the single most emblematic unit of Suleiman's 1529 army, yet the besiegers are Camel Riders, Light Cavalry and Cavalry Archers, an entirely avoidable misrepresentation of an assault force that attacked the Carinthian Gate on foot with sappers and janissary storming parties.

Player 1's text promises 'German Landsknechts and Spanish arquebusiers', but not one gunpowder unit is placed for the defenders; the Teutons have access to Hand Cannoneers, so the arquebusiers named in the dialogue are contradicted by Crossbowmen on the wall.

Suleiman is represented by a KING unit rather than a renamed generic military unit; a renamed Champion, Janissary or cavalry hero of the era would have read as a commander instead of a defenceless chess piece parked in the camp.

Two Bombard Cannons overstate Ottoman artillery: the heavy siege train bogged down on the march and Suleiman had only light guns before Vienna, which is precisely why he relied on mining the Carinthian Gate.
No Danube or any water feature appears on the map, although the river and the Ottoman crossing/supply problem were defining features of the siege's geography.
The '29 September first great assault' is invented - the Ottoman army only completed its investment around 27 September, and the recorded assaults fall on 6, 9, 11, 12 and 14 October.
Salm's wounding is placed at the 11 October assault; he was in fact struck by rock splinters during the final 14 October assault and died of the wound the following March, which the narration omits.
1414 oak trees dominate a 144x144 map, giving the approaches to a Danube-plain city a north-European forest character rather than open siege ground and vineyard slopes.
strengths: Civilizations are explicitly and correctly assigned: Teutons for the German-officered Viennese garrison, Turks for the Ottomans.
192 Stone Walls, a Keep, Guard Towers and a single named Gate build a genuine medieval curtain rather than a token wall, matching Vienna's outdated pre-bastion defences.
The Ottoman camp is dressed with Pavilion, twelve tents, a bonfire and a flag, an appropriate depiction of a besieging army encamped outside the walls.
The countermine subplot is the historically decisive mechanic: a sapper who must be intercepted before reaching the Carinthian Gate, with a scripted breach and reinforcement wave on failure.

Victory is gated purely on surviving to a deadline, correctly encoding a siege the defenders had only to outlast, while defeat triggers on three Ottoman units reaching the city's heart - the loss Vienna actually faced.
The escalating dated assaults and the closing narration attributing withdrawal to autumn rains, mud and exhausted supplies reflect the real causes of the Ottoman retreat.
justification: The scenario gets the frame right: Teutons behind 192 tiles of stone wall against Turks in a tented camp, a countermine race at the Carinthian Gate, and a victory condition that is simply outlasting the besieger with defeat if Ottoman troops reach the city centre - exactly the goal Salm's garrison faced. It fails on force composition: the Turks field no Janissaries or infantry of any kind, only camels, light cavalry and cavalry archers, and the defenders' promised Spanish arquebusiers are represented by Crossbowmen even though Teuton Hand Cannoneers were available. Dating is loose - a 'first great assault' on 29 September did not occur, and Salm's wound belongs to the 14 October assault, not the 11th - but the narration's account of mining, escalating assaults, rain, mud and supply failure is substantially true to the sources.
